section.title: The Altar and the Curses
section.sectionRationale: This chapter enacts a covenant renewal ceremony at Shechem: the law written on plastered stones, an altar of unhewn stone for atonement, and twelve curses recited antiphonally between Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal, each sealed by Israel's own binding 'Amen,' showing the nation publicly agreeing that these curses are the just due of the sins named.
section.thesis: Before entering the land, Israel must publicly inscribe the law, build an altar of unworked stone, and recite twelve curses against specific hidden and social sins, each answered by the whole nation's 'Amen,' binding Israel to acknowledge that breaking the covenant justly brings God's curse, the very curses chapter 28 will describe in full and Christ will one day bear.
section.frameNote: Four movements: writing the law on large plastered stones; building an altar of uncut stones for burnt and peace offerings; the tribes divided between Mount Gerizim for blessing and Mount Ebal for curse; and the Levites' recitation of twelve curses, each sealed by the people's own 'Amen'.

units.label: The law written in stone
units.note: plain to see, for all to read

verses.text: Then Moses and the elders of Israel commanded the people: "Keep all the commandments I am giving you today.
And on the day you cross the Jordan into the land that the LORD your God is giving you, set up large stones and coat them with plaster.

Write on them all the words of this law when you have crossed over to enter the land that the LORD your God is giving you, a land flowing with milk and honey, just as the LORD, the God of your fathers, has promised you.
And when you have crossed the Jordan, you are to set up these stones on Mount Ebal, as I am commanding you today, and you are to coat them with plaster.
Moreover, you are to build there an {{mizbeach|altar}} to the LORD your God, an altar of stones. You must not use any iron tool on them.
You shall build the altar of the LORD your God with uncut stones and offer upon it burnt offerings to the LORD your God.
There you are to sacrifice your peace offerings, eating them and rejoicing in the presence of the LORD your God.
And you shall write distinctly upon these stones all the words of this law."

units.label: This day you have become the LORD's people

verses.text: Then Moses and the Levitical priests spoke to all Israel: "Be silent, O Israel, and listen! This day you have become the people of the LORD your God.
You shall therefore obey the voice of the LORD your God and follow His commandments and statutes I am giving you today."

units.label: Blessing from Gerizim, curse from Ebal

verses.text: On that day Moses commanded the people:
"When you have crossed the Jordan, these tribes shall stand on Mount Gerizim to bless the people: Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Joseph, and Benjamin.
And these tribes shall stand on Mount Ebal to deliver the curse: Reuben, Gad, Asher, Zebulun, Dan, and Naphtali.

units.label: Twelve curses, and Israel's Amen
units.note: the nation agrees to the law's justice

verses.text: Then the Levites shall proclaim in a loud voice to every Israelite:

'{{arur|Cursed}} is the man who makes a carved idol or molten image, an abomination to the LORD, the work of the hands of a craftsman, and sets it up in secret.' And let all the people say, '{{amen|Amen}}!'
'Cursed is he who dishonors his father or mother.' And let all the people say, 'Amen!'
'Cursed is he who moves his neighbor's boundary stone.' And let all the people say, 'Amen!'
'Cursed is he who lets a blind man wander in the road.' And let all the people say, 'Amen!'
'Cursed is he who withholds justice from the foreigner, the fatherless, or the widow.' And let all the people say, 'Amen!'
'Cursed is he who sleeps with his father's wife, for he has violated his father's marriage bed.' And let all the people say, 'Amen!'
'Cursed is he who lies with any animal.' And let all the people say, 'Amen!'
'Cursed is he who sleeps with his sister, the daughter of his father or the daughter of his mother.' And let all the people say, 'Amen!'
'Cursed is he who sleeps with his mother-in-law.' And let all the people say, 'Amen!'
'Cursed is he who strikes down his neighbor in secret.' And let all the people say, 'Amen!'
'Cursed is he who accepts a bribe to kill an innocent person.' And let all the people say, 'Amen!'
'Cursed is he who does not put the words of this law into practice.' And let all the people say, 'Amen!'

arur.gloss: Cursed. The recurring refrain 'cursed is...' pronounced by the Levites over specific sins, met each time by the whole people's binding 'Amen,' shows Israel publicly agreeing that these curses are the just due of the sin named.

amen.gloss: Truly, so be it, from a root meaning firm or faithful. Israel's repeated response binds the whole nation to agree that these curses justly apply to whoever commits these sins, including, ultimately, themselves.

mizbeach.gloss: Altar, from a root meaning to slaughter or sacrifice. Built here of uncut, natural stones untouched by human tool, so that the place of atonement owes nothing to human craft or achievement.

basic.context: Before crossing into the land, Israel is to hold a covenant renewal ceremony at Shechem: writing the law on large plastered stones for all to read, building an altar of natural, unhewn stones for offerings, dividing six tribes to Mount Gerizim for blessing and six to Mount Ebal for curse, and having the Levites recite twelve specific curses against hidden sins and social injustice, each one sealed by the whole nation's own spoken 'Amen.'
basic.hermeneutics: This is a real, one-time covenant ceremony for Israel's specific entry into the land, historically situated at Shechem between two actual mountains; its enduring message, however, that God's people publicly and knowingly agree to the justice of His curse against sin, sets up the whole logic Paul later uses in Galatians 3:10-13 to explain why Christ had to bear the law's curse.
basic.originalLanguages: Each curse begins arur, cursed, and the people answer amen, truly, so be it, literally agreeing that the curse is deserved. The mizbeach, altar, must be built of uncut stones, so that atonement owes nothing to human craftsmanship or achievement.
basic.typology: Israel's own spoken agreement to the law's curses anticipates Paul's argument in Galatians 3:10, that everyone who does not keep the whole law is under a curse, a curse Christ Himself takes on at the cross, becoming a curse for us, Galatians 3:13, quoting Deuteronomy's own language of hanging on a tree.
basic.christ: Galatians 3:10-13 draws directly on this covenant curse logic: since no one keeps the whole law perfectly, everyone stands under its curse, but Christ 'redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us,' so that the blessing promised to Abraham might reach the nations.
basic.god: God requires His people to know and own the seriousness of covenant unfaithfulness before they even enter the land, not surprising them later; He is scrupulously fair, requiring Israel's own informed 'Amen' to the justice of the curse before ever executing it.
basic.crossReferences: Galatians 3:10-13 draws directly on the logic of curse and blessing established here. Joshua 8:30-35 records Israel actually carrying out this ceremony at Mount Ebal after entering the land. Nehemiah 10:29 shows Israel later binding themselves again with a curse and an oath to keep the law. Revelation 22:3 promises 'no longer will there be any curse,' the final undoing of what is set up here.
basic.oneStory: Israel publicly agrees that breaking covenant deserves God's curse, setting up the entire logic of blessing and curse that chapter 28 will unfold in detail, and that the gospel will finally resolve when Christ bears the curse His people had already agreed they deserved.

context.literary:
This chapter opens the covenant renewal unit that runs through chapter 30, and it is built from four distinct acts rather than one continuous scene, writing the law on plastered stones, verses 1 to 8, a summons to silence and a declaration of new identity, verses 9 to 10, the division of tribes between two mountains, verses 11 to 13, and the recitation of twelve curses with the people's answering "Amen," verses 14 to 26. The narrator moves from writing to silence to geography to speech, engaging Israel's eyes, ears, feet, and mouths in turn, so the whole nation's body, not merely its ears, is bound into the ceremony.

The command to inscribe the law is given three times across verses 1 to 8, Moses commands "today," the writing happens "when you have crossed," and the instruction to "write distinctly" closes the unit, a deliberate repetition that functions like a legal document restating its own terms to make sure nothing is missed before a monumental, one time act.

The twelve curses of verses 15 to 26 are arranged in a rough but noticeable order, beginning with an offense against God alone, secret idolatry, and ending with an offense against the whole law, "cursed is he who does not put the words of this law into practice," verse 26, framing eleven specific hidden sins inside a twelfth, comprehensive one. Between the two poles sit sins within the family, verses 16 and 20 to 23, and sins against a neighbor's property, safety, and justice, verses 17 to 19 and 24 to 25, so the list itself moves outward from God, to family, to neighbor, to the law as a whole, mapping the entire shape of covenant obligation in miniature.
context.historical:
Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal form a natural amphitheater above the ancient city of Shechem, close enough together that a crowd standing on one slope could plausibly hear a recitation from the other, which is likely why the ceremony was staged there rather than at some other pass in the hill country. Shechem itself already carried patriarchal weight before Israel arrived, Abram built his first altar in Canaan near its oak of Moreh, Genesis 12:6 to 7, and Jacob purchased land and raised his own altar there generations later, Genesis 33:18 to 20, so Moses stages Israel's covenant ceremony at a site already soaked in memories of earlier promises kept.

Plastering large stones and inscribing the law on them, verses 2 to 4, mirrors a practice known from other ancient monumental inscriptions, where treaties, victories, or laws were displayed publicly on prepared stone or stucco surfaces so anyone literate, and anyone who heard it read, could confirm exactly what had been agreed. A law inscribed in public, rather than kept only on a scroll in priestly custody, could not later be quietly reinterpreted by those in power.

The altar's uncut stones, verse 5, repeat an instruction already given at Sinai, that no tool may shape stones used for the LORD's altar, Exodus 20:25, a rule that kept Israel's central act of worship from ever becoming a display of human craftsmanship or artistic achievement.

Joshua carries out this exact ceremony almost immediately after Israel enters the land, building the altar, writing the law, and dividing the tribes between the same two mountains, Joshua 8:30 to 35, confirming this was not a merely theoretical instruction but one Israel's first generation in Canaan actually obeyed to the letter.
context.canonical:
Paul builds the heart of his Galatian argument directly on the final curse of this chapter. "Cursed is he who does not put the words of this law into practice," verse 26, becomes, quoted almost word for word, the foundation of his claim that "all who rely on works of the law are under a curse," Galatians 3:10, since no one keeps the entire law without failure. From there Paul moves to the cross, where Christ "redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us... for it is written, cursed is everyone who is hung on a tree," Galatians 3:13, deliberately quoting Deuteronomy 21:23, so two distinct verses from Deuteronomy's legal core meet at the foot of the cross in Paul's argument.

The ceremony itself becomes a fixed reference point for later covenant renewal. Joshua repeats it precisely, Joshua 8:30 to 35, and centuries later, after the exile, the returned community again binds itself "with a curse and an oath to follow the Law of God," Nehemiah 10:29, showing Israel kept returning to the same pattern, public inscription, public assent, whenever covenant loyalty needed to be publicly renewed.

The final curse of verse 26 also echoes forward into the Psalms, where the righteous man delights in a law he can actually keep, Psalm 1:2, in implicit tension with a law that, taken as a whole demand, no one keeps perfectly, a tension the New Testament resolves only in Christ's own perfect obedience credited to those who trust Him, Romans 5:19.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses wants Israel to enter the land having personally, audibly agreed that the law's penalties are just, so no future generation could claim it never understood, or never consented to, what covenant breaking would cost. By requiring each Israelite's own voice in the "Amen," he turns abstract statutes into a personal oath every worshiper speaks over their own head.

He deliberately weights the ceremony toward curses aimed at sins easily hidden, secret idolatry, a boundary stone moved under cover of night, a bribe paid quietly, because human courts require evidence and witnesses, and a society can only govern what it can see. Moses wants Israel to know that the LORD's justice reaches further than any court's, into exactly the corners a clever sinner assumes are safe.

Finally, by inscribing the law publicly on stone at the very entrance to the land, rather than leaving it only in priestly or royal custody, Moses intends Israel's obedience to rest on a law everyone could see and read for themselves, not on the private interpretation of whoever held power, protecting ordinary Israelites from having the law's actual demands hidden or twisted against them later.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The specific ceremony, plastered stones at a particular pair of mountains, an altar built exactly there, twelve curses recited in that exact order, describes a one time historical event tied to Israel's entry into one particular land under one particular covenant. No church today reenacts a stone writing ceremony at Shechem, and the New Testament nowhere instructs believers to do so.

What carries forward is the principle Paul extracts from it, that a law demanding perfect obedience, spoken over by anyone who takes its terms seriously, becomes a curse for every real sinner who fails to keep all of it, Galatians 3:10. This is not a rule believers still enact but a diagnosis Scripture still uses, explaining why the law could never itself save and why Christ's bearing of that exact curse, rather than believers reciting it again, is the New Testament's actual answer to what this chapter sets in motion.

debates.question: Why does the list of curses in verses 15-26 focus especially on hidden sins?

views.label: Because human courts cannot try what only God can see
views.case: Most of these curses, secret idolatry, moving a boundary marker at night, secretly striking a neighbor, bribery, describe sins easily hidden from human courts, so the curse invokes God's own certain judgment where human justice cannot reach.

views.label: Because the whole list functions as a summary of the law's basic demands
views.case: Ending with "cursed is he who does not put the words of this law into practice," verse 26, the list may function as a representative summary of covenant obedience as a whole, not merely a catalogue of undetectable crimes.

debates.bearing: Both readings agree the final curse, verse 26, generalizes the whole law's claim on Israel, which Paul quotes directly in Galatians 3:10 to show that no one is justified by law keeping alone.

debates.question: Why does the ceremony split the tribes six and six between Gerizim and Ebal rather than by geography or convenience alone?

views.label: Grouped by descent from Leah and Rachel against the servant wives
views.case: The tribes on Gerizim for blessing, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Joseph, and Benjamin, descend mainly from Leah and Rachel; several tribes on Ebal for curse descend from the servant women Bilhah and Zilpah, or, in Reuben's case, carry an earlier disgrace, Genesis 49:3-4, suggesting the placement reflects each tribe's standing within Jacob's family.

views.label: A practical division for filling two mountainsides
views.case: Others see the split as simply the most workable way to arrange roughly equal numbers facing each other across the valley, without reading any deeper theological statement about the tribes' standing into the specific assignment given here.

debates.bearing: Either way, the text never explains the assignment outright, so any theological weight placed on which tribe stood where should be held loosely; what the ceremony unmistakably teaches is that every tribe, without exception, stood under both the promise of blessing and the warning of curse.

study.originalLanguages:
The chapter's key refrain word, arur, cursed, verses 15 through 26, sits in the same root family as its opposite in the very next chapter, barak, blessed, Deuteronomy 28:2 to 6, so chapters 27 and 28 form one linguistic unit, a nation cursed here for specific hidden sins is offered blessing there for comprehensive obedience, two Hebrew word families holding the whole covenant together.

Israel's answering word, amen, verses 15 through 26, comes from the same root as the verb "to believe," he'emin, the word used of Abram, "Abram believed the LORD, and it was credited to him as righteousness," Genesis 15:6. Twelve times the people speak a word built on the same root as Abraham's own faith, so Israel's response to the law's curses is not mere acknowledgment but something closer to a sworn declaration of trust, staking their own faithfulness on knowing exactly what unfaithfulness would cost.

The altar of verse 5, mizbeach, comes from a root meaning to slaughter, and must be built of uncut stones untouched by any iron tool, a rule already given at Sinai, Exodus 20:25, and expressed there and here with the same underlying concern, a place of atonement must owe nothing to human skill or craftsmanship, since what happens there depends entirely on what God provides, not on what human hands can shape.

Verse 8's command to "write distinctly," using a rare Hebrew verb elsewhere translated "explain," echoes the very first verse of Moses' entire address, "Moses began to explain this law," Deuteronomy 1:5. The same verb frames the whole legal core of Deuteronomy, what Moses first explained aloud at the beginning of the book, Israel now inscribes permanently in stone at its end, so speech becomes monument.

Finally, the plaster coating the stones, sid, verses 2 and 4, is the same word used elsewhere for burned lime, a substance made durable and white by fire, so the law is set down not on bare, weathered rock but on a bright, prepared surface meant to hold every letter legible for as long as the plaster itself lasted, a small detail underlining how badly Moses wanted this law actually read, not merely possessed.

The double command of verse 9, "be silent, O Israel, and listen," pairs two imperatives rarely joined this way elsewhere in the Torah, silencing the whole assembly's own voice before it is given, twelve times over, the single word it is allowed to answer back, amen.

typology.type: Israel's spoken Amen to the law's curse, Deuteronomy 27:15-26
typology.fulfillment: Paul quotes the chapter's final, summarizing curse almost verbatim, "cursed is everyone who does not continue to do everything written in the Book of the Law," to argue that all who rely on law keeping stand under its curse, Galatians 3:10, since no one keeps the whole law without failure. Israel's own sworn "Amen" becomes, centuries later, the very indictment Paul uses to show every human being's need for a righteousness that does not come from law keeping. The type is a legal principle carried forward rather than a picture awaiting fulfillment, since Paul treats the curse as a present verdict on all humanity, not a shadow of one event.

typology.type: The altar of unhewn stone, Deuteronomy 27:5-6
typology.fulfillment: An altar owing nothing to human tools pictures atonement as entirely God's own provision rather than any achievement of the worshiper, a principle Christ's own atonement fulfills without qualification, since He is Himself "not with the blood of goats and calves, but... with His own blood," Hebrews 9:12. No human craft contributed anything to the cross, just as no chisel touched these stones. The correspondence is thematic rather than a stated New Testament fulfillment, since Scripture never explicitly reads this altar as a picture of Christ, but the shared logic, atonement owing nothing to human skill, is exact.

typology.type: The law written on stone at the border of the land, Deuteronomy 27:2-8
typology.fulfillment: A law inscribed on stone that Israel could not keep perfectly anticipates Paul's contrast between the old covenant, "the ministry of death, chiseled in letters on stone," and the new covenant of the Spirit, which gives life, 2 Corinthians 3:6-7. Christ inaugurates a covenant whose terms are not carved on rock for a nation to read but written on the heart itself, "I will put My law within them and write it on their hearts," Jeremiah 31:33, quoted directly in Hebrews 8:10. The stones of Shechem are answered not by better engraving but by an entirely different kind of writing.

typology.type: The curse hung on the mountain answered by the curse hung on a tree
typology.fulfillment: This chapter's curses, sworn over Israel at two mountains, and Deuteronomy 21:23's warning that "anyone who is hung on a tree is under God's curse," meet directly in Paul's account of the cross, where Christ "redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us... cursed is everyone who is hung on a tree," Galatians 3:13. The curse Israel agreed applied to every lawbreaker becomes, at Calvary, a curse the sinless Christ takes on Himself, so that "the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles," Galatians 3:14, in the very next verse.

study.christ:
Galatians 3 is where this chapter most directly meets Christ. Paul quotes its closing curse almost word for word, "cursed is everyone who does not continue to do everything written in the Book of the Law," Galatians 3:10, and argues that since no one keeps the whole law perfectly, everyone who relies on law keeping for right standing before God stands, in fact, under the very curse Israel swore to at Shechem. The nation's own twelve "Amens" become, centuries later, humanity's own indictment.

Paul then reaches for a second verse from this same section of Deuteronomy to explain how the curse is finally answered. Deuteronomy 21:23 calls anyone hung on a tree accursed, and Paul applies it directly to the cross, "Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us, for it is written, cursed is everyone who is hung on a tree," Galatians 3:13. The one man who never earned a single curse under this chapter's terms takes on Himself the entire weight of every curse it names, so that, Paul continues in the very next verse, "the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles... so that by faith we might receive the promise of the Spirit," Galatians 3:14.

The altar of uncut stone also points toward Christ by contrast and correspondence together. Just as no chisel could touch the stones of Israel's atonement, so no human effort contributed anything to the atonement Christ accomplished; He alone is "the source of eternal salvation," Hebrews 5:9, offered once for all rather than repeated at an altar built anew in every generation.

Finally, the law written on stone at Shechem finds its answer not in a better inscription but in a different kind of writing altogether. What Moses had Israel carve into plaster, God promises one day to write directly onto the heart, "I will put My law within them and write it on their hearts," Jeremiah 31:33, a promise Hebrews applies to the new covenant Christ inaugurates, 8:10, so obedience no longer depends on stones Israel could see but on a Spirit believers actually receive.
study.god:
God, in this chapter, refuses to let His people claim ignorance. He has the law written where every eye can see it and read aloud in every ear, and He requires each Israelite's own voice in agreeing that its penalties are deserved, so no one standing at Shechem that day could later say the terms were unclear or unfairly imposed on them without consent.

He is a God whose justice reaches beyond what any human court can verify. Most of the twelve curses target exactly the sins a clever, careful sinner could hide, a secretly moved boundary stone, a bribe paid in private, a neighbor struck down where no witness saw it, and the curse form itself declares that God's own knowledge, not merely human testimony, stands behind every one of these judgments. Nothing done in secret against a neighbor is actually secret from Him.

He is scrupulously fair. Rather than pronouncing sentence and waiting for Israel to discover the terms later through hard experience, He lays out the exact stakes before Israel ever crosses the Jordan, and He binds Israel's own agreement into the ceremony itself, wanting a covenant people who enter knowingly rather than blindly.

He is the God who provides atonement without needing anything from human hands. The altar built at the very site of this curse ceremony, of stone untouched by iron tool, says that even as Israel agrees to the law's severe terms, God has already made provision for approaching Him that owes nothing to human craft or achievement, mercy built into the very ceremony that pronounces judgment.

And He is holy in a way that refuses to rank sins by how easily they are noticed. Idolatry practiced in secret, verse 15, sits in the same list as bribery, sexual sin, and murder, showing that what matters to God is not whether a sin becomes public but whether it is committed at all, a standard no human court, however diligent, could ever fully enforce, and one only God is qualified to judge.

crossReferences.note: Paul quotes this chapter's closing curse almost word for word to argue that everyone who relies on keeping the law stands under its curse, since no one obeys "everything written in the Book of the Law" without failure.

Christ becomes a curse for His people by being hung on a tree, taking on Himself the exact penalty this chapter and Deuteronomy 21:23 describe, so the blessing promised to Abraham might reach the nations by faith.
Declares that anyone hung on a tree is under God's curse, the verse Paul quotes alongside this chapter's curse language in Galatians 3:13 to explain what happened to Christ at the cross.

Joshua carries out this exact ceremony almost immediately after Israel crosses the Jordan, building the altar, writing the law, and dividing the tribes between Gerizim and Ebal precisely as Moses commanded here.

The returned exiles bind themselves again with a sworn oath to follow the Law of Moses, showing this chapter's pattern of public, spoken covenant commitment recurring whenever Israel's loyalty needed renewing.
Gives the same instruction for an altar of unhewn stone untouched by any tool, the rule this chapter's altar of verses 5 and 6 repeats decades later at the very edge of the promised land.

Paul contrasts the old covenant, "the ministry of death, chiseled in letters on stone," with the new covenant of the Spirit, drawing a direct line from stones like these to the greater glory of the covenant Christ inaugurates.

Quotes Jeremiah's promise that God will write His law on His people's hearts rather than on stone, describing the new covenant Christ mediates as the true answer to what Moses only inscribed in plaster.

Records Jacob purchasing land at Shechem and building his own altar there generations before Moses chose the same site for Israel's covenant ceremony, tying this chapter to a place already marked by patriarchal worship.
Promises that in the new creation "no longer will there be any curse," the final and complete undoing of the very word, cursed, pronounced twelve separate times over Israel at Mount Ebal.

study.oneStory:
This chapter stages, in one afternoon at Shechem, the choice the whole Bible keeps setting before humanity since Eden, blessing for trusting and obeying God, curse for turning away from Him. Israel's spoken "Amen" over twelve specific sins is a kind of national echo of Adam and Eve's own fall, an agreement, however unwitting, that disobedience truly deserves what it brings, sealed this time with full knowledge rather than a serpent's deception.

The altar of unhewn stone standing beside the curses is not incidental. Even as Israel agrees to the law's severe terms, God has already provided a place of atonement that depends on nothing Israel's own hands have shaped, a small, physical reminder, right at the moment of the law's harshest demand, that mercy has already been built into the relationship before a single curse is pronounced.

The chapter's closing curse, aimed at anyone who fails to keep the whole law, sets up the very problem the rest of Scripture works to solve. Paul reads it as evidence that the law could only ever curse, never save, and it takes the whole rest of the story, culminating in Christ hung on a tree bearing exactly this curse, to answer what Israel agreed to at Shechem.

The story does not end at Ebal. What Israel spoke over stone plastered white, God later promises to write directly on the heart, Jeremiah 31:33, and the New Testament announces that promise kept in Christ, Hebrews 8:10. And what this chapter pronounces twelve times, cursed, Revelation reverses completely in the very last chapters of the Bible, promising a city where "no longer will there be any curse," Revelation 22:3, so the mountain of curse at Shechem finds its final answer not in another mountain but in a city where the curse itself has been undone forever.

quiz.q: What were the Israelites commanded to write on large stones coated with plaster, verses 2-3?

options.text: All the words of this law.
options.note: Verses 3 and 8 state this explicitly.

options.text: The names of the twelve tribes only.
options.note: The text specifies the words of the law, not merely tribal names.

options.text: A list of Canaanite cities to conquer.
options.note: The text specifies the law, not a military list.

options.text: Nothing; no writing is commanded.
options.note: Verses 2-3 and 8 give an explicit command.

quiz.q: What kind of stones must the altar be built from, verses 5-6?

options.text: Uncut, natural stones; no iron tool may be used on them.
options.note: Verses 5-6 state this explicitly.

options.text: Finely carved and polished stones.
options.note: The text explicitly forbids using any iron tool to cut or shape the stones.

options.text: Stones brought from Egypt.
options.note: The text specifies natural, unhewn stones with no reference to their origin.

options.text: No instruction is given about the altar's stones.
options.note: Verses 5-6 are explicit.

quiz.q: Which six tribes stood on Mount Gerizim to pronounce the blessing, verse 12?

options.text: Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Joseph, and Benjamin.
options.note: Verse 12 names these tribes explicitly.

options.text: Reuben, Gad, Asher, Zebulun, Dan, and Naphtali.
options.note: These six tribes instead stood on Mount Ebal for the curse, verse 13.

options.text: All twelve tribes stood together on Gerizim.
options.note: The text explicitly divides the tribes between two mountains.

options.text: No tribes are named for this ceremony.
options.note: Verses 12-13 name all twelve tribes across the two mountains.

quiz.q: What did the people say after each curse was pronounced by the Levites?

options.text: 'Amen!'
options.note: This response follows every curse from verse 15 through verse 26.

options.text: Nothing; they remained silent.
options.note: The text explicitly records the people's spoken response each time.

options.text: 'We refuse this curse.'
options.note: The text records agreement, 'Amen,' not refusal.

options.text: No response is recorded.
options.note: Every curse is followed by the people's explicit 'Amen.'

quiz.q: What does the final curse in verse 26 declare?

options.text: Cursed is he who does not put the words of this law into practice.
options.note: Verse 26 states this explicit, summarizing curse, later quoted by Paul in Galatians 3:10.

options.text: Cursed is he who lives outside the land of Israel.
options.note: The final curse concerns obedience to the law, not geography.

options.text: Cursed is he who is born a foreigner.
options.note: The final curse concerns disobedience to the law, not ethnicity.

options.text: No final, summarizing curse is given.
options.note: Verse 26 gives an explicit, comprehensive final curse.

questions: Israel had to write the law in plain sight and publicly agree, 'Amen,' to the justice of its curses. Where do you need to be more honest with yourself about what God's word actually requires, rather than keeping it vague?

The altar was built of unworked stone, so atonement owed nothing to human skill. Where are you tempted to think your own effort or achievement earns you standing before God, rather than resting in what Christ has done?
Many of the curses in this chapter target sins done in secret, moving a boundary marker, a hidden bribe, a secret attack. What sin are you hiding that you assume no one, including God, can see?
Christ became a curse for us so that the blessing of Abraham might come to us. How does knowing Jesus already bore the exact curse you deserved change the weight of guilt you carry today?
Israel's whole nation answered 'Amen' together, publicly agreeing to the same standard. Who in your life could you agree with, out loud, to pursue faithfulness to God together?

translationNotes.note: Some ancient manuscript traditions read 'Mount Gerizim' rather than 'Mount Ebal' for the location of the stones and altar; the Masoretic Hebrew text followed by the BSB reads Ebal, consistent with Ebal being the mountain of curse in verse 13.

The list of twelve curses is not exhaustive of the whole law but functions representatively, especially highlighting sins easily hidden from human courts, culminating in the sweeping final curse of verse 26 quoted by Paul in Galatians 3:10.
Paul quotes this verse in Galatians 3:10 to argue that everyone who relies on keeping the law is under its curse, since no one keeps 'everything written in the Book of the Law' perfectly.
